title: Planner overrides and why a plan failed

blocks.text: 14.1.6 Planner Overrides and Why a Plan Failed
With calendars in place (the lesson *Weather and access windows: calendars and optional work*), GridCap's vegetation planner started using the plan every week, and two requests followed:

Sometimes I know something the model doesn't. A crew is already on site near C17, so start it there in week 0. The county closes the road to C17 until October, so leave it. A landowner complained, so trim C02 first. I need to tell the planner these things and have it plan *around* them.

And when it can't, "INFEASIBLE" is not an answer. Last week I forced in five circuits after a storm and got an empty plan and that one word. Tell me *which* of my decisions clash, in my words, so I know what to give up.

The first request is **overrides**: a planner's decision that the plan must keep. The second is **explanation**: when no plan keeps every rule, a short list of the rules that cannot hold together. (GridCap and its seasons are fictional, generated by the project's seeded generator.) This lesson takes the project from `steps/05` to `steps/06`.
The Planner Takes No Instructions, and Its Failure Says Nothing

`steps/05` has one input, the season. A planner who wants C17 left out can only edit the season's data (delete the circuit, or set its window to nothing), which loses the record that it was a decision, by whom and why, and makes the next season's data wrong. And when a season is infeasible, `make_plan` returns `Plan("INFEASIBLE")`: a true statement that tells the planner nothing. CP-SAT proved that the rules cannot all hold, and the code threw that proof away.
An Override Is One More Rule, and Every Rule a Planner Can Change Sits Behind a Literal

Three override kinds cover the requests: **pin** (trim this circuit, optionally on this crew and from this week), **skip** (leave it for next season) and **force** (trim it this season, anyhow). Each is a rule of the same shape as a must: a few rows that hold when the override is in force.
For the explanation, the design options (lessons 9.1.2, 9.1.4 and 9.1.5 compared them):

rows: Check the data before solving (lesson 9.1.2): sum the musts' costs, compare with the budget
instant, and the message writes itself
only for conflicts someone thought of in advance; two pins that overlap on one crew, or a pin outside a window, need the model
Elastic rows: add slack to every rule and minimize the slack (lesson 9.1.4)
says how far each rule is from holding
changes the objective and the model's meaning; the planner wants names, not amounts
One literal per changeable rule, solved as **assumptions**; CP-SAT names a set of them enough for the proof; a deletion filter makes it minimal (lessons 4.6.2 and 9.1.5)
the rules that clash, by name, from the real model
chosen: it finds any conflict the model can prove, and needs no change to the model's meaning

blocks.text: An **assumption** is a literal the solver must take as true for this solve (lesson 4.6.2). Every rule a planner can change, each must, the budget and each override, is written as rows enforced by its own literal. A normal solve fixes all those literals to true, so the model means exactly what it meant before. When the season is infeasible, a second solve passes the literals as assumptions, and `sufficient_assumptions_for_infeasibility` returns those the proof used. That set is enough, but not always the smallest (lesson 4.6.2), so a **deletion filter** tries each name in turn: drop it, and if the rest still cannot hold, it stays dropped.

The hard facts stay hard: windows, crews' weeks off, one trim per crew at a time. They are physics, not decisions; an explanation that says "or let K1 work two circuits at once" is not one a planner can act on.
The Model
The lesson *Weather and access windows: calendars and optional work*'s model, with every changeable rule behind a literal, and the overrides. In full:

**Sets.** As in the lesson *Weather and access windows: calendars and optional work*: $`C`$, $`K`$, weeks, $`M`$, windows $`W_c`$, time off $`O_k`$; and ← *this lesson* the overrides $`V`$, split into pins $`V^{\text{pin}}`$ (each with a circuit, and optionally a crew $`k_v`$ and a first week $`f_v`$), skips $`V^{\text{skip}}`$ and forces $`V^{\text{force}}`$; $`c_v`$ is override $`v`$'s circuit.
**Parameters.** $`\text{cost}_c`$, $`B`$, $`w_c`$, $`R_c(e)`$, $`D`$, as before.

**Variables.** $`t_c`$, $`p_{c,k}`$, $`s_{c,k} \in S_c`$, $`I_{c,k}`$, $`e_c`$, $`\rho_c`$ as before; ← *this lesson* a rule literal $`\ell_r \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every changeable rule $`r`$: one per must, one for the budget, one per override.
**Objective.**
\min \; \sum_{c \in C} \rho_c
**Constraints.** The rows of the lesson *Weather and access windows: calendars and optional work* (once, ends, waits, risk, crew) unchanged, and:

The last row belongs to the planning solve. The explaining solve leaves it out and passes the $`\ell_r`$ as assumptions instead. A pin's week is stated on the end, $`e_c = f + w_c`$, because the end is one variable per circuit, whatever crew does the work.
The Change, File by File

`planner.py` held the plan, the model and the solve, and now needs a fourth job, explaining. That is one job too many for one file, so this step splits it: **`model.py`** (new) holds the model, **`explain.py`** (new) the explanation, and `planner.py` keeps the plan and the solve.
**`vegcrew/data.py`.** `Override`, a frozen dataclass like the others, which can say itself in the planner's words:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/data.py -->

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Override:
    """A planner's decision the plan must keep: pin a trim, skip a circuit, or force one in."""
    kind: str                       # "pin", "skip" or "force"
    cid: str
    crew: str | None = None         # pin: this crew (None: any crew)
    start: int | None = None        # pin: this first week (None: any week)
    reason: str = ""

    def says(self) -> str:
        where = "".join([f" on {self.crew}" if self.crew else "", f" from week {self.start}"
                         if self.start is not None else ""])
        what = {"pin": f"trim {self.cid}{where}", "skip": f"leave {self.cid} for next season",
                "force": f"trim {self.cid} this season"}[self.kind]
        return f"{what} ({self.reason or 'no reason given'})"
The `reason` is carried into every message. A planner reading "override 4: trim C01 this season (regulator letter)" knows which decision it was and why it was made.
**`vegcrew/model.py`, new.** `crew_ids`, `horizon`, `start_domain`, `TrimModel` and `build`, moved from `planner.py`. `TrimModel` gains the rule literals and their words, and a method that makes one:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/model.py -->

rules: dict[str, cp_model.IntVar] = field(default_factory=dict)                   # name -> literal
    says: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)                                # name -> words

    def rule(self, name: str, says: str) -> cp_model.IntVar:
        """A literal that switches one of the planner's rules on; the rows it guards hold only if it is 1."""
        self.rules[name] = self.model.new_bool_var(name)
        self.says[name] = says
        return self.rules[name]
In `build`, the must row of the lesson *Weather and access windows: calendars and optional work*, `tm.model.add(t == 1)`, is now enforced by a rule literal, and so is the budget:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/model.py -->
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/model.py -->

tm.model.add(sum(c.cost * tm.trimmed[c.cid] for c in season.circuits) <= season.budget).only_enforce_if(
        tm.rule("budget", f"the season's budget is ${season.budget:,}k"))                # budget
The budget's words print it with a thousands comma, as the report does: `the season's budget is $962k`, or `$1,000k` for a budget of 1000. Each override adds its rows behind its own literal:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/model.py -->
If a pin names a crew for a circuit that has no crew options (no window fits it), the crew row is skipped; $`t_c = 1`$ alone then cannot hold, and the explanation names the pin.
**`vegcrew/explain.py`, new.** Three small functions. `holds` asks whether a set of rules can all hold at once, with one worker, stopping at the first plan found, since only yes or no matters:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/explain.py -->

def holds(tm: TrimModel, names: list[str]) -> bool:
    """Can these rules all hold at once? One worker, stopped at the first plan: only yes or no matters."""
    tm.model.clear_assumptions()
    tm.model.add_assumptions([tm.rules[n] for n in names])
    solver = cp_model.CpSolver()
    solver.parameters.num_workers = 1
    solver.parameters.stop_after_first_solution = True
    return solver.solve(tm.model) != cp_model.INFEASIBLE

`conflict(tm)` asks CP-SAT for its set, filters it, and returns the rules that remain in the order they were made. It is the explanation, and the page leaves its code to the practice. Its contract is the method of *An Override Is One More Rule, and Every Rule a Planner Can Change Sits Behind a Literal* above, in four steps:

items: solve once with every rule literal of `tm.rules` as an assumption, after clearing any assumptions already on the model, with one worker (assumptions need a single worker); if the status is not INFEASIBLE, every rule can hold, and the answer is `[]`;
run the deletion filter over that set: for each name in it, in turn, if the set without that name still cannot hold (`holds` answers False), leave the name out for good;
return the names that remain, sorted in the order the rules were made, which is the order of `tm.rules`.

blocks.text: The solver returns indices of literals (its docstring says "the indices of the infeasible assumptions"), not the literals, so map each literal's `.index` back to its rule name. The rules are made in a fixed order, each must in the inventory's order, then the budget, then the overrides in the order given, and the explanation lists its rules in that order, whatever order the solver named them in. The third function, `why_infeasible`, builds the model and maps the conflict's names to the planner's words:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/explain.py -->

**`vegcrew/planner.py`.** Shorter: it imports the model, and `make_plan` gains an `overrides` argument (a stub in `steps/05`), a data check before any model is built, the "every rule holds" row, and the explanation on failure:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/vegcrew/planner.py -->

problems = check_overrides(season, overrides)
    if problems:
        raise ValueError("; ".join(problems))
    tm = build(season, overrides)
    tm.model.add_bool_and(list(tm.rules.values()))     # every rule holds
    solver = cp_model.CpSolver()
    solver.parameters.max_time_in_seconds = TIME_LIMIT
    solver.parameters.num_workers = WORKERS
    status = solver.status_name(solver.solve(tm.model))
    if status == "INFEASIBLE":
        return Plan(status, explanation=tuple(why_infeasible(season, overrides)))

`check_overrides` catches what is wrong with an override as data (an unknown circuit, crew or kind, a week outside the season) and returns every problem at once. These are typing mistakes, not conflicts, and the model is the wrong place to find them (lesson 9.1.2): a pin naming circuit Z9 would otherwise fail as a `KeyError` deep in `build`.

**`vegcrew/report.py`.** When a plan has an explanation, the report prints it as a list headed "these rules cannot all hold; change one of them". `steps/06` also carries a stub `record.py` for the lesson *The same plan every run: determinism and regression tests*.
Overrides Have a Price, and a Clash Names Its Rules
`overrides_demo.py` plans the small season with `steps/06` (`WORKERS` set to 1, so the output repeats). First with two overrides the plan can keep, the road closure and the school:

no overrides: OPTIMAL, risk carried $4,571k
season small-54: 20 circuits, budget $962k, crews 2, weeks 24
status OPTIMAL: 9 trims, cost $954k, risk carried $5,197k
  K1 666666600.xx44444446666.  C16:0-6 C10:7-8 C04:12-18 C06:19-22
  K2 22233555511111xxxx5555..  C02:0-2 C03:3-4 C15:5-8 C01:9-13 C05:18-21
the two overrides cost $626k of risk

C17 is gone (skipped), C02 runs on K2 from week 0 (pinned), and everything else moved around them. The plan is OPTIMAL *for the season with those overrides*: the overrides are rules, so it is the best plan that keeps them, and it carries $626k more than the plan without them. That number belongs in front of whoever asked for the overrides.
Then two pins that cannot both hold: C17 (seven weeks) on K1 from week 0, and C02 on K1 from week 5:

status INFEASIBLE: 0 trims, cost $0k, risk carried $0k
these rules cannot all hold; change one of them:
  - override 1: trim C17 on K1 from week 0 (crew already on site)
  - override 2: trim C02 on K1 from week 5 (complaints near the school)

Two rules, in the planner's words, with their reasons. Of the season's five changeable rules (two musts, the budget and these two pins), the other three are not mentioned, because they are not part of the clash.
Then the storm week: five forced circuits on top of the two musts.

status INFEASIBLE: 0 trims, cost $0k, risk carried $0k
these rules cannot all hold; change one of them:
  - C05 is overdue and must be trimmed this season
  - C16 is overdue and must be trimmed this season
  - the season's budget is $962k
  - override 1: trim C08 this season (storm damage)
  - override 2: trim C11 this season (fire-risk area)
  - override 3: trim C14 this season (customer complaints)
  - override 4: trim C01 this season (regulator letter)
  - override 5: trim C19 this season (new subdivision)
the arithmetic: 85 + 213 + 178 + 105 + 112 + 179 + 117 = $989k > $962k
rules behind literals: 8; named by the solver: 8; after the deletion filter: 8

All eight rules are in the conflict: seven circuits cost $989k, $27k over the budget, and dropping any one of them (the cheapest is $85k) or raising the budget by $27k ends it. The list is long because the conflict is: every rule is needed for the proof, and the deletion filter confirmed each one. Here the solver's set was already minimal; lesson 4.6.2 shows a case where it is not, which is why the filter stays.
Six Tests: Three Overrides, Two Clashes, One Data Check
`steps/06` adds `tests/test_overrides.py`. The clash tests check the exact words, because the words are the feature:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/tests/test_overrides.py -->

def test_two_pins_that_overlap_on_one_crew_are_named_together():
    s = season(1000, ("A", 10, 50, 3), ("B", 10, 40, 3), ("C", 10, 30, 1), crews=1, months=2)
    plan = make_plan(s, (Override("force", "C", reason="storm damage"),
                         Override("pin", "A", crew="K1", start=0, reason="crew is nearby"),
                         Override("pin", "B", crew="K1", start=2, reason="landowner asked")))
    assert plan.status == "INFEASIBLE"
    assert plan.explanation == ("override 2: trim A on K1 from week 0 (crew is nearby)",
                                "override 3: trim B on K1 from week 2 (landowner asked)")

Override 1 (force C) is there on purpose: it is a rule the explanation must *leave out*. Without it, an explanation that listed every override would pass. The data check is tested on its own, without a solve:
<!-- snapshot: steps/06/tests/test_overrides.py -->

def test_overrides_that_name_nothing_are_refused_before_the_solve():
    s = season(1000, ("A", 10, 50, 3), crews=1, months=1)
    assert check_overrides(s, (Override("pin", "Z9", crew="K7", start=40), Override("trim", "A"))) == [
        "override 1: no circuit Z9", "override 1: no crew K7", "override 1: week 40 is outside the season",
        "override 2: unknown kind 'trim'"]

The rest: a pin lands on its crew and week; a skip leaves the best circuit out; a force brings in one the model would leave; and a must beyond the budget names the must and the budget, but not the other must, which fits. `step06.py`:

  FAILED test_overrides::test_a_skip_leaves_the_circuit_for_next_season  AssertionError: assert ['A'] == ['B']
  FAILED test_overrides::test_force_trims_a_circuit_the_model_would_leave  AssertionError: assert ['A'] == ['B']
  FAILED test_overrides::test_overrides_that_name_nothing_are_refused_before_the_solve  assert [] == ['override 1:... kind 'trim'"]
  FAILED test_overrides::test_two_pins_that_overlap_on_one_crew_are_named_together  AssertionError: assert 'OPTIMAL' == 'INFEASIBLE'
  ...and 23 of 23 earlier tests pass
against steps/06 (after): 29 of 29 pass
`steps/05`'s stubs accept the overrides and ignore them, so each test fails on what the override should have changed.
The Step Split the Planner Into Three Files

code, steps/05 -> steps/06 (lines, functions; blanks and comments left out):
  __init__.py     4   0  ->    4   0
  __main__.py    16   1  ->   16   1
  data.py        53   4  ->   59   5  changed
  explain.py      0   0  ->   37   3  new
  generate.py    49   2  ->   49   2
  model.py        0   0  ->   74   5  new
  planner.py     92   6  ->   65   2  changed
  record.py       0   0  ->   10   3  new
  report.py      18   1  ->   22   1  changed
  package       232  14  ->  336  22
  tests         166  23  ->  201  29  (lines, tests)

The package grew by 104 lines, the most of any step so far, and for the first time by new files rather than longer ones. (`record.py` is the 10-line stub for the lesson *The same plan every run: determinism and regression tests*.) Each file now has one reason to change: `model.py` when a rule changes, `explain.py` when the way conflicts are found changes, `planner.py` when the solve or the plan changes. `build` is still the longest function, at about 45 lines, and it reads top to bottom like the formulation. The complexity added is real: a model that can switch its own rules off is a model whose meaning depends on how it is solved, which is why the "every rule holds" row sits in `make_plan`, in one line, with a comment.

**Practice.** This lesson's project practice starts from the whole package as `steps/05` left it. Submit grades it with the practice's own `tests/` (the tests of `steps/06`) and checks that `main.py`, which plans the tiny season, prints the practice's `expected/report.txt`. This step's `main.py` also plans the tiny season with one override it can keep and with two pins that clash; the practice's statement gives both sections.

Summary

items: **The planner took no instructions, and its failure said nothing.** Overrides had to be data edits, and INFEASIBLE threw CP-SAT's proof away.
**An override is one more rule, and every rule a planner can change sits behind a literal.** The planning solve fixes the literals to true; the explaining solve passes them as assumptions.
**Overrides have a price** ($626k on the small season for two of them), **and a clash names its rules,** minimal by a deletion filter, in the planner's words with their reasons.
**Six tests,** including one that checks an innocent rule is left out of the explanation.

blocks.text: Reference

**Further reading:** [ortools 9.15.6755 on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/ortools/9.15.6755/) (the pinned release; the docstrings of `CpModel.add_assumptions` and `CpSolver.sufficient_assumptions_for_infeasibility` in its `ortools.sat.python.cp_model`, read in the runner); lesson [4.6.2](../17-cpsat-tuning-and-diagnostics/README_4.6.2.md) (assumptions, and a deletion filter that shrinks the named flags); lesson [9.1.5](../37-infeasibility/README_9.1.5.md) (CP-SAT assumptions as a conflict finder, and the order of the filter); lesson [9.1.6](../37-infeasibility/README_9.1.6.md) (turning a conflict into a planner message); the lesson [Manual overrides as bounds, with an audit trail](../45-scenario-workflow/README_12.1.2.md) in section 12 (overrides as bounds, with an audit trail).
Challenges

items: Run the storm-week overrides with a $1,000k budget. Predict the status, then the plan's cost.
The deletion filter tries rules in the solver's order. Change it to try overrides first. On which season could that give a different, equally minimal, explanation?
Add a fourth override kind, "not before week N". Write its rows and the test that pairs an allowed and a refused plan.

blocks.text: Design Note: Keep Physics Hard and Decisions Soft

Only rules a planner can change got literals: musts, the budget, overrides. Windows, time off and "one trim per crew at a time" did not. An explanation is useful only if every rule it names is one the reader can act on; "or let K1 work two circuits at once" is not. The line also keeps the explaining solve small: eight literals to filter, not one per row. If an explanation ever needs to name a window ("C01's ground is too wet in week 2"), give windows a literal then, and decide on purpose that a window is negotiable.
The Full Programs

**overrides_demo.py.** Plans the small season with `steps/06`, with overrides it can keep and two sets it cannot, and compares the solver's conflict set with the filtered one (*Overrides Have a Price, and a Clash Names Its Rules*). *Try:* Move the C02 pin to week 7. Predict whether the clash ends.

**step06.py.** Runs this lesson's tests against `steps/05` and `steps/06` and counts the code (*Six Tests*). *Try:* Remove the deletion filter's loop on a copy of `steps/06` and predict which test can fail.
**snapshots.py.** Imports a snapshot, runs one snapshot's tests on another's code, counts its code.
